paragraphs: Nonnegative matrix factorization approximates a data matrix using smaller factors whose entries cannot be negative. Many algorithms enforce that restriction at every optimization step. This paper argues that staying inside the allowed region can obstruct progress, slowing convergence or steering the search toward less useful stationary points.

The proposed exterior method, eNMF, separates finding a low-rank approximation from enforcing nonnegativity. It starts with the optimal unconstrained factorization, then rotates the factors toward the nonnegative region. Its iterative updates converge to boundary stationary points satisfying the relevant constrained optimality conditions; this is not a guarantee of finding a global optimum.

The geometric perspective also explains how apparently different factorizations can be equivalent. Across 400 experiments, different algorithms tended toward equivalent factors in 99% of cases. Against 81 algorithm-and-initialization combinations, eNMF reports up to 30% lower reconstruction error at equal runtime and up to 150% speedup at equal error. Improvements in audio processing and recommendation suggest that its optimization benefits can carry through to downstream tasks.
icml-2026-an-exterior-method-for-nonnega.tldr: eNMF approaches nonnegative factorization from outside the feasible region, improving reconstruction quality and optimization speed in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Approximate nearest neighbor search finds close matches without exhaustively comparing a query with every stored item. This paper treats search speed as one part of a broader engineering problem: useful indexes must also be quick to build, economical in memory, adaptable to high dimensions and different result counts, and able to accept new items.

Projection-Augmented Graph, or PAG, combines a graph index with projection methods. Its central mechanism uses statistical tests based on projections to compare exact and approximate distances asymmetrically. These comparisons reduce unnecessary exact distance calculations. Three components integrate that mechanism into index construction and searching, addressing both stages of the retrieval process.

Experiments on six datasets report a better tradeoff between queries per second and recall, with speedups reaching five times those of HNSW. PAG also provides fast indexing and a moderate memory footprint, remains robust as dimensions and requested result counts increase, and supports online insertions. The contribution is therefore a combination of retrieval performance and operational flexibility across the tested workloads.
icml-2026-approximate-nearest-neighbor-s.tldr: PAG uses projection-based statistical tests inside a graph index to accelerate retrieval while supporting practical indexing and update requirements.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can produce descriptions that do not match the visual evidence. Existing remedies often adjust how much attention goes to images versus language, or use contrastive decoding, which the abstract identifies as doubling inference time. This paper examines another aspect of the problem: the spectral structure of visual information as it flows through attention.

The authors identify two hallucination patterns, called Perceptual-Semantic Dissociation and Localized Fixation. They develop FLASH, a method that changes attention during decoding without additional training or contrastive decoding. A Spectral Vortex Score identifies visual attention heads, and adaptive spectral modulation then adjusts the information flowing through those heads.

The approach matters because it changes the structure of visual processing rather than relying solely on the total attention assigned to visual tokens. The experiments report a better balance between performance and efficiency than the compared state-of-the-art methods. This supports spectral modulation as a practical intervention for reducing hallucinations while avoiding the particular inference overhead associated with contrastive decoding.
icml-2026-beyond-attention-imbalance-mit.tldr: FLASH reduces vision-language hallucinations by modifying the spectral structure of visual attention during decoding, without training or contrastive decoding.

paragraphs: An adversarially perturbed image can make CLIP both less accurate and more confident. The paper highlights this combination as a reliability problem beyond classification errors: uncertainty should ordinarily reflect increased difficulty, yet the authors frequently observe it decreasing under attack. Simply matching prediction scores between clean and perturbed images can overlook this problem.

The proposed fine-tuning objective addresses accuracy and uncertainty together. It represents CLIP outputs as concentration parameters of a Dirichlet distribution, allowing the representation to express both relationships among semantic predictions and the magnitude of confidence. Training aligns these richer distributions under perturbations instead of anchoring individual prediction scores alone.

Across multiple zero-shot benchmarks, the method substantially improves uncertainty calibration while retaining competitive adversarial robustness and preserving accuracy on clean inputs. These findings indicate that robustness and confidence quality can be addressed within one objective. The practical contribution is a model whose confidence better reflects its predictive reliability in the evaluated adversarial settings, alongside its ability to classify perturbed images.
icml-2026-calibrating-uncertainty-for-ze.tldr: A distribution-based fine-tuning objective improves CLIP’s uncertainty calibration under adversarial perturbations while preserving clean accuracy.

paragraphs: Antibody sequences contain information about the evolutionary process that produced them. Models that treat sequences as independent examples can miss this information, while classical evolutionary models have limited ability to represent interactions between mutations. CoSiNE combines explicit evolutionary dynamics with the flexibility of a neural network.

The method uses a continuous-time Markov chain whose behavior is parameterized by a deep network. The authors prove that it approximates sequential point mutation to first order, with an error bound that grows quadratically with evolutionary branch length. This gives a precise qualification to the approximation while allowing it to capture epistasis, where a mutation’s effect depends on other sequence positions.

Empirically, CoSiNE outperforms leading language models at zero-shot variant effect prediction by separating selection from context-dependent somatic hypermutation. The paper also introduces Guided Gillespie, which uses classifier guidance to steer sampling at inference time toward antibody binding affinity for particular antigens. Together, the contributions connect modeling how antibodies evolve with directing that modeled process toward an engineering objective.
icml-2026-conditionally-site-independent.tldr: CoSiNE models antibody evolution with a neural continuous-time process and uses guided sampling to optimize binding affinity toward specific antigens.

paragraphs: Adapting a language model from a few examples does not always require updating its underlying parameters. Prompt-based methods instead optimize a trainable prompt or prefix. This paper focuses on how that trainable context begins: conventional approaches often initialize it with tokens that have little relevance to the task.

Context Tuning initializes the prompt or prefix using task-specific demonstrations. Those examples give the model relevant information from the outset and engage its existing ability to learn from examples in context. Optimization then operates on this task-informed context while leaving the model parameters unchanged. The central intervention is therefore a change in the starting material for adaptation.

Evaluations on CrossFit, UnifiedQA, MMLU, BIG-Bench Hard, and ARC show improvements over traditional prompt-based adaptation. The method also achieves accuracy competitive with Test-Time Training at substantially higher training efficiency. These results suggest that choosing a useful initialization for trainable context can materially improve few-shot adaptation, making better use of capabilities already present in the language model.
icml-2026-context-tuning-for-in-context-.tldr: Context Tuning improves few-shot adaptation by initializing trainable prompts with relevant demonstrations while keeping model parameters fixed.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves language-model reasoning using responses whose outcomes can be checked. However, generated responses can differ substantially in training value. Treating them uniformly and discarding them after one use can introduce noisy supervision and waste useful experience.

This paper makes rollout scheduling a contextual bandit problem. Each rollout becomes an option the scheduler can select, and its reward is the performance improvement induced between consecutive optimization steps. A neural scheduler uses this formulation both to choose useful responses within a prompt’s group and to decide when historical responses should be reused. Selection and reuse therefore share one learning framework.

The theoretical analysis provides sublinear regret bounds and shows that a larger rollout buffer improves the achievable performance upper bound. That upper-bound result does not itself guarantee that every buffer expansion improves realized performance. Experiments on six mathematical reasoning benchmarks nevertheless show consistent gains in performance and training efficiency across multiple RLVR optimization methods, supporting the value of learning which generated experience to train on.
icml-2026-contextual-rollout-bandits-for.tldr: A contextual bandit scheduler improves RLVR training by learning which responses to select and when to reuse past rollouts.

paragraphs: Language-model unlearning aims to reduce the influence of selected training data, including private or inappropriate material. A common strategy increases prediction loss on the examples to be forgotten. The paper argues that this can remove more useful behavior than intended, producing excessive forgetting and reducing the model’s overall utility.

DareU changes the optimization target to data attribution. It uses reinforcement learning to reduce how strongly generated responses are attributed to the owners of the designated forget data. This reframes the learning signal around the relationship between outputs and the targeted data source, rather than relying on prediction loss alone to drive forgetting.

In the experiments, an LLM classifier provides an efficient approximation of attribution. Using that signal, DareU outperforms the compared unlearning baselines while balancing forgetting quality with retained model utility. The stated result supports attribution rewards as a useful alternative training objective. Its empirical evidence specifically concerns the classifier-based attribution approximation used in those experiments, which is an integral part of how the framework is evaluated.
icml-2026-de-attribute-to-forget-for-llm.tldr: DareU uses reinforcement learning to reduce attribution to targeted training-data owners, improving the reported balance between forgetting and model utility.

paragraphs: Label distribution learning predicts how support is spread across labels instead of selecting just one. However, conventional measures of prediction quality can overlook whether that support is divided between semantically opposing labels. The paper calls this property divisiveness and treats it as information relevant to practical decision risk.

The authors define a divisiveness measure with a formal polarity-monotonicity property, giving the concept an explicit mathematical foundation. They then show that conventional loss functions are inconsistent with divisiveness error. Consequently, optimizing familiar distribution losses does not necessarily preserve the particular pattern of disagreement that the new measure captures.

Directly minimizing divisiveness error introduces an adversarial gradient problem. The proposed framework addresses this with a pairwise divisiveness loss that is an unbiased estimator of the original error. Experiments support the method’s effectiveness. The contribution is a learning objective that explicitly preserves an aspect of label distributions that standard metrics can miss, making the training target more attentive to disagreement between opposing outcomes.
icml-2026-divisiveness-consistent-label-.tldr: This framework measures and preserves disagreement between opposing labels through a divisiveness-aware training objective.

paragraphs: Mixed integer linear programs are commonly solved with branch-and-bound, where branching choices strongly affect the search. Neural branching methods must interpret nodes at different depths, even though node meaning and feature distributions vary across the tree. Training also faces a shortage of upstream nodes and expensive strong-branching examples.

SC-MILP addresses these difficulties through dynamic grouping and targeted data augmentation. It groups nodes according to their feature distributions, then uses stratified contrastive training to learn detailed representations sensitive to search depth. This makes the representation-learning process account for variation among nodes rather than treating all training examples as interchangeable.

An upstream augmentation procedure generates both theoretically equivalent and perturbed MILP instances to address the scarcity and imbalance of early-tree training data. Experiments cover synthetic and real-world benchmarks, including large problems, and report better branching accuracy and shorter solving times. Gains are particularly strong at upstream nodes. The results connect improved training coverage and depth-sensitive representations with more effective branching decisions during optimization.
icml-2026-dynamic-stratified-contrastive.tldr: SC-MILP improves learned branching through depth-sensitive contrastive training and augmentation aimed at scarce upstream search nodes.

paragraphs: Federated learning becomes harder when participating clients differ both in their data and in their models. Even when they exchange useful knowledge, fine-grained feature mismatches can prevent their representations from aligning. This weakens the shared model’s generalization and each client’s ability to benefit from collaboration.

FedARC combines a lightweight shared feature extractor with client-specific fusion. A trainable projector integrates local and global embeddings, while adaptive residual compensation corrects mismatches at the feature level. Semantic anchors align representations across clients to make aggregation more stable. These mechanisms address both the information clients share and how each client incorporates that information.

The authors prove a nonconvex convergence rate of O(1/T). Experiments on five public benchmarks compare FedARC with nine state-of-the-art heterogeneous federated-learning baselines and report average-accuracy improvements of up to 2.63%, while keeping communication and computation efficient. The findings support explicit feature correction and semantic alignment as complementary tools for transferring knowledge when both client data and model structures vary.
icml-2026-fedarc-anchor-guided-residual-.tldr: FedARC aligns heterogeneous clients through shared features, local fusion, residual correction, and semantic anchors, improving benchmark accuracy efficiently.

paragraphs: Federated clients can each find locally flat solutions while their combined model remains poorly aligned with the global objective. The paper attributes this discrepancy to differences in clients’ data distributions, which produce mismatched loss landscapes. Promoting local flatness alone therefore need not deliver global flatness or better generalization.

FedScar tracks a geometric bias accumulated over training history to capture persistent curvature differences across clients. A variance-aware injection mechanism uses this information to direct local updates toward regions that are flat for the global objective. The correction targets a systematic mismatch in optimization geometry, supplementing the usual effort to bring client parameters into agreement.

The authors interpret the method through a Split-Dual ADMM formulation that jointly addresses parameter consensus and geometric alignment. Under severe data heterogeneity, experiments report consistently smaller flatness discrepancies and better generalization than the compared state-of-the-art approaches, without additional communication overhead. The results suggest that accounting for how client objectives curve can improve the usefulness of flatness-oriented federated optimization.
icml-2026-fedscar-correcting-geometric-b.tldr: FedScar corrects persistent differences in client loss geometry to improve global flatness and generalization without extra communication.

paragraphs: A convincing website interface can conceal missing backend behavior or data storage. This paper targets the broader challenge of generating functioning full-stack applications, where an agent must manage data flow, understand dependencies, and locate bugs across a repository. It combines an agent framework, a learning method, and a benchmark.

FullStack-Dev coordinates multiple agents for planning, editing, code navigation, and bug localization. FullStack-Learn improves the underlying language model by back-translating crawled and synthesized website repositories into learning material. FullStack-Bench evaluates frontend, backend, and database functionality separately, making success across the application’s layers visible rather than judging the interface alone.

FullStack-Dev improves over the previous state of the art by 8.7%, 38.2%, and 15.9% on those three groups of tests, respectively. Self-improvement through FullStack-Learn raises a 30B model’s performance by 9.7%, 9.5%, and 2.8%. Together, these results support both the development framework and repository-derived learning as ways to improve functional web application generation.
icml-2026-fullstack-agent-enhancing-agen.tldr: FullStack-Agent combines coordinated coding agents, repository-derived learning, and functional testing to improve generated frontend, backend, and database behavior.

paragraphs: AI-generated annotations can expand the information available for causal inference, but simply pooling them with human labels can introduce bias. Treating generated outputs as stand-ins for true labels can also be inappropriate. Generative Augmented Inference instead treats those outputs as potentially informative features from which human labels can be learned.

GAI uses flexible nonparametric methods to model the relationship between AI outputs and human labels. This allows generated information to be high-dimensional and to have a more general relationship with the target than a direct label approximation. The framework establishes consistent estimation, valid inference, and asymptotic normality for the combined-data approach.

Its efficiency result has an explicit condition: under random labeling, GAI strictly improves asymptotic efficiency over human-only estimation whenever AI outputs inform the true labels. Real-world experiments also report lower estimation error and better confidence intervals than human-only and PPI-based methods across diverse generative sources. The contribution is a statistical framework for using generated information without requiring it to behave like a trustworthy replacement label.
icml-2026-generative-augmented-inference.tldr: GAI uses AI outputs as informative features for human labels, enabling valid inference and conditional efficiency gains from combined human and AI data.

paragraphs: Biophysically detailed neural models have irregular, tree-shaped computational structures that fit poorly with the dense operations favored by general deep-learning frameworks. HelioX tackles this mismatch by designing GPU execution around biological structure, with the aim of making both simulation and training efficient.

The framework implements custom fused CUDA kernels for Dendritic Hierarchical Scheduling and for propagating its gradients. Handling the gradient computation directly removes the runtime overhead of generic automatic differentiation. It also runs spike generation and equation assembly concurrently through multiple GPU streams. These choices connect the biological model’s structure to the hardware’s execution strategy.

Experiments report orders-of-magnitude speed improvements over NEURON and better speed and scalability than prior GPU solvers. The authors also train deep biophysical MLPs and whole-brain-scale circuits, including the BAAIWorm C. elegans model, on one consumer-grade GPU. These demonstrations show that specialized execution can expand the scale of biophysically detailed models that can be trained, alongside accelerating their simulation.
icml-2026-heliox-a-gpu-native-framework-.tldr: HelioX uses biology-aware GPU kernels to accelerate detailed neural simulation and enable large biophysical models to train on a single consumer GPU.

paragraphs: Self-attention is usually described as a query looking up keys through normalized scores. This paper develops another interpretation: an autoregressive attention head acts like a two-layer neural network whose weights are constructed from the preceding context. As the context grows, so does the intermediate representation associated with attention scores.

Under this view, standard activations such as ReLU or GLU can select information from context-dependent memory without making the selection weights a probability distribution. HyperMLP and HyperGLU build on this formulation by learning dynamic mixing across both features and sequence positions. A reverse-offset layout organizes temporal mixing by lag, aligning it with the autoregressive use of preceding context.

The paper provides theoretical characterizations of this structure’s expressive capacity and implications. Empirically, both models consistently outperform strong softmax-attention baselines with matched parameter budgets. These findings support the proposed interpretation as an architectural design principle: viewing attention through familiar neural-network operations leads to alternatives that improve sequence modeling in the reported comparisons.
icml-2026-hypermlp-an-integrated-perspec.tldr: HyperMLP and HyperGLU reinterpret attention as a context-generated neural network and outperform matched-budget softmax-attention baselines in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Predicting systems that evolve across space and time is difficult when detailed simulation is expensive and measurements are sparse, noisy, or irregular. MERLIN learns observation functionals: compact quantities derived from the system’s spatial state whose evolution is approximately linear. This provides a low-dimensional representation that can expose principal modes of the dynamics.

A finite collection of learned quantities does not generally preserve perfectly closed linear dynamics. The framework addresses that loss using the Mori–Zwanzig formalism, adding memory terms that allow predictions to depend on past behavior. The memory correction complements the linear backbone instead of requiring the reduced state alone to explain every future change.

Function encoders accept partial, irregular observations without depending on a particular discretization. Function decoders reconstruct the spatial state at arbitrary query points and resolutions. Training with linear constraints supports interpretability and reduced-order modeling, while the memory correction enables stable long-horizon rollouts even with very small latent spaces. The approach joins flexible handling of spatial measurements with a compact dynamical model that retains useful historical information.
icml-2026-interpretable-functional-koopm.tldr: MERLIN combines approximately linear learned dynamics with memory corrections to predict spatial systems from irregular observations at arbitrary resolutions.

paragraphs: Preference datasets for image generation usually retain a prompt and the preferred and rejected images. For rectified-flow models, this leaves out information about the particular initial noise that generated each image. Estimating training trajectories through independent forward noising can then mismatch the generation dynamics and introduce avoidable variance.

PNAPO retains the paired prior noises alongside the preference examples. Because rectified-flow trajectories are nearly straight, it estimates intermediate states by interpolating between the recorded noise and its resulting image. This restricts the space of possible trajectory estimates and yields a tighter surrogate objective for learning from preferences. The approach is specialized to the structure of rectified flow.

The method also changes its regularization dynamically according to the reward difference between preferred and rejected outputs and the progress of training. This is intended to improve stability and sample efficiency. Experiments on state-of-the-art rectified-flow text-to-image backbones report consistent preference-metric improvements with substantially less training computation, supporting the value of retaining generation history in offline preference data.
icml-2026-offline-preference-optimizatio.tldr: PNAPO records the initial noises behind image preference pairs to improve rectified-flow alignment while reducing training computation.

paragraphs: The densest k-subgraph problem asks for a densely connected selection of k graph vertices and is computationally hard. A recent penalty-based relaxation showed promising empirical behavior, but its success lacked a rigorous explanation. This paper analyzes the relationship between that continuous optimization problem and the original discrete one.

First, the authors prove that the relaxation is tight: its global maximum value equals the original problem’s global maximum value. They then characterize stationary points. Integral stationary points are local maxima, while non-integral stationary points are strict saddles with explicitly positive curvature. Thus, stationary solutions that do not correspond to discrete selections have a mathematically identifiable escape direction.

Using that geometry, the authors develop a saddle-escaping Frank–Wolfe algorithm and prove exact convergence to an integral local maximum in finitely many steps. The distinction between local and global is central: matching global objective values across formulations does not make the algorithm globally optimal. The result explains how continuous optimization can terminate at a valid discrete local solution with a finite-step guarantee.
icml-2026-on-densest-k-subgraph-mining-a.tldr: The paper proves a tight densest-subgraph relaxation and finite-step convergence of a saddle-escaping algorithm to an integral local maximum.

paragraphs: Diffusion and flow models commonly generate images through repeated sampling steps and operate in a latent representation. Pixel MeanFlow, or pMF, brings together two departures from that setup: producing an image in one step and working directly without a latent space. The paper’s main design choice concerns what the network predicts and where its error is measured.

The network predicts an image, following the assumption that images lie on a low-dimensional manifold. Its loss, however, is defined in velocity space through MeanFlow. A transformation connects the image prediction to the average velocity field, allowing the output representation and training objective to be designed separately while remaining linked.

On ImageNet, the method reports FID scores of 2.22 at 256-by-256 resolution and 2.48 at 512-by-512 resolution for one-step, latent-free generation. These results support the feasibility of combining direct pixel generation with one-step sampling. The contribution is the formulation that makes those choices work together, especially the separation between an image-shaped prediction target and a velocity-based learning signal.
icml-2026-one-step-latent-free-image-gen.tldr: Pixel MeanFlow enables one-step image generation without latents by combining image prediction with a MeanFlow loss in velocity space.

paragraphs: This paper revisits the basic structure of long-term forecasting rather than adding architectural complexity. Its Variance Reduction Hypothesis proposes that generating and combining multiple forecasts is essential for reducing neural forecasters’ inherent uncertainty. The hypothesis motivates a design that embeds forecast combination within one network.

Boosted Direct Output combines the causal organization of autoregressive forecasting with the stability of direct-output forecasting. The resulting model implicitly combines forecasts while retaining a streamlined structure. The authors also use parameter smoothing to stabilize optimization and reduce a gap between validation performance and test generalization, addressing training behavior alongside forecast construction.

With these changes, a direct temporal MLP outperforms recent complex state-of-the-art models on nearly all evaluated benchmarks. The authors also empirically support their variance-reduction hypothesis and establish a dynamic performance bound. The findings indicate that forecast organization and optimization stability can account for substantial performance gains, even in a simple architecture. The hypothesis’s support is empirical, and the reported benchmark advantage is broad but not universal.
icml-2026-renf-rethinking-the-design-of-.tldr: ReNF improves long-term forecasting through implicit forecast combination and parameter smoothing, allowing a simple temporal MLP to beat complex models on nearly all tested benchmarks.

paragraphs: Learning from pixels requires a reinforcement-learning agent to discover which visual information matters for obtaining reward. Auxiliary tasks can help build representations, but reconstructing images or predicting states does not directly match the goal of maximizing return. Return-Critic changes the auxiliary target to the episode’s return.

The framework samples a subset of frames from an episode and passes them through the same visual encoder used for representation learning. A lightweight Transformer then predicts the episode return from those encoded frames. This training signal encourages the encoder to retain information relevant to task outcomes. Its attention weights also highlight important frames, providing a mechanism for prioritized learning.

Experiments evaluate the approach in online learning on DMControl and offline learning on V-D4RL. The authors report substantial improvements in sample efficiency, including an average 68% performance increase across nine challenging DMControl tasks. These findings support aligning representation learning with return prediction so that visual features are trained around the same outcome the agent ultimately seeks to improve.
icml-2026-return-critic-bridging-goal-di.tldr: Return-Critic trains visual representations to predict episode return, improving reinforcement-learning sample efficiency in online and offline benchmarks.

paragraphs: Safety alignment can be weakened by subsequent harmful fine-tuning. This paper observes that persistent fine-tuning can circumvent defenses imposed on parameters, gradients, or internal representations. Its analysis attributes this to redundancy in a high-dimensional parameter space, where optimization can move in directions orthogonal to the imposed constraints while recovering harmful behavior.

Safety Bottleneck Regularization focuses on the unembedding layer, which the paper identifies as a geometric bottleneck. It anchors final hidden states for harmful queries to corresponding states from the safety-aligned model. The defense therefore constrains a representation closely involved in producing responses, with the goal of preserving safe behavior during continued harmful fine-tuning.

Experiments show that a single safety anchor is sufficient to bring the Harmful Score below 10 while maintaining competitive performance on benign downstream tasks. This is a sufficiency result in the evaluated settings, rather than a universal protection guarantee. The findings support the paper’s argument that the location and geometry of a safety constraint can matter for its resistance to persistent fine-tuning.
icml-2026-safety-anchor-defending-harmfu.tldr: Safety Bottleneck Regularization anchors final hidden states to preserve safe responses under persistent harmful fine-tuning in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Functional brain networks vary between individuals, and that variation can interfere with learning patterns useful for psychiatric disorder identification. SI-IGCL addresses this with two stages: self-supervised pretraining to reduce dependence on subject identity, followed by supervised fine-tuning for disorder classification.

Its inverse contrastive objective pushes apart embeddings from the same subject and pulls together embeddings from different subjects. This reshapes the representation space toward patterns shared across individuals. An auxiliary correction term helps prevent early optimization plateaus, while a reconstruction constraint preserves network structure and discriminative information. These components balance removing subject-specific variation with retaining useful classification signals.

A Hierarchical Topology Enhanced Transformer models shared functional patterns at multiple structural levels. The final supervised stage adds a classifier to those learned representations. The authors report that the method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in their experiments. The contribution is a coordinated representation-learning strategy that explicitly addresses subject variation while preserving brain-network information needed for the downstream identification task.
icml-2026-si-igcl-subject-invariance-awa.tldr: SI-IGCL learns brain-network representations that reduce subject-specific variation while preserving information useful for psychiatric disorder classification.

paragraphs: In a sufficiently large world, an agent’s competence is uneven. A uniform worst-case guarantee can obscure whether the agent understands transitions crucial to a goal or fails on irrelevant parts of the environment. This paper formalizes that limitation by proving that general agents are not universal in the big-world regime.

Structural certification evaluates the internal world model transition by transition. It connects bounded goal-conditioned performance with guarantees on individual entries of that model. Constructive algorithms use deep compositional goals to filter specific transitions, allowing behavioral performance to provide localized evidence about the agent’s understanding of the world.

For an agent general on those goals, the authors prove a structural world-model error bound of O(1/n) + O(δ). They also establish tightness in a small-δ regime whose existence the certification guarantees. These results identify particular transitions where long-horizon planning is reliable, giving certification a more selective role than an all-purpose competence claim. The practical significance is the ability to distinguish reliable pieces of a world model from failures elsewhere.
icml-2026-world-models-in-pieces-structu.tldr: Structural certification translates goal-conditioned performance into local world-model guarantees that identify transitions supporting reliable long-horizon planning.
